reference.source: Textbook of Autoinflammation / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: A type I interferonopathy caused by gain-of-function mutations in IFIH1 (MDA5) or DDX58 (RIG-I), cytosolic nucleic-acid sensors
Hallmarks are abnormal dental development with early tooth loss, aortic and vascular calcification, and skeletal abnormalities
Cardiovascular calcification of the aorta and heart valves can occur unusually early and cause serious complications
Dental features include delayed or abnormal dentition, dysplastic teeth, and premature loss of teeth
Skeletal manifestations may include osteopenia, acro-osteolysis, and widened medullary cavities
A raised interferon signature supports the diagnosis alongside genetic confirmation
JAK inhibition targeting the interferon pathway is being used to address the underlying interferon-driven inflammation
reference.pathophysiology: Singleton-Merten syndrome is caused by gain-of-function mutations in IFIH1 (encoding MDA5) or DDX58 (encoding RIG-I), cytosolic sensors of viral nucleic acids. The mutant sensors are inappropriately activated, driving constitutive production of type I interferons even without genuine infection. Chronic interferon signalling promotes ectopic calcification of the aorta and cardiac structures, disturbs tooth and bone development, and causes systemic inflammatory features. The interferon-dominant mechanism links the dental, cardiovascular, and skeletal manifestations and provides the rationale for JAK inhibition to reduce interferon signalling.
additionalDifferentials: Other type I interferonopathies (Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome, SAVI, CANDLE)
Metabolic bone disease of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Genetic testing for IFIH1 (MDA5) and DDX58 (RIG-I) mutations
Cardiovascular imaging for aortic and valvular calcification
Dental and orthopantomogram assessment of dentition
Skeletal radiographs for osteopenia and acro-osteolysis
Echocardiography to assess cardiac structure and function
redFlags: Progressive aortic or valvular calcification threatening cardiac function
Early cardiovascular compromise in a child or young adult
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is largely determined by cardiovascular calcification, which can cause serious morbidity; interferon-directed therapy may modify disease, but established calcification and dental loss are difficult to reverse.
pitfalls: Overlooking early vascular calcification as an incidental or age-related finding
Attributing dental abnormalities to a primary ectodermal disorder alone
Not requesting an interferon signature when an interferonopathy is possible
Missing the genetic link between IFIH1/DDX58 variants and the multisystem phenotype
management: JAK inhibitor therapy (such as baricitinib or ruxolitinib) to dampen the type I interferon signalling that drives the disease
Cardiovascular management of aortic and valvular calcification with antihypertensives, heart failure therapy and surgical or valve intervention when calcification is severe
Dental care for dysplastic dentition and early tooth loss, including prostheses and regular dental review
Bone health support with management of osteopenia and acro-osteolysis and physiotherapy
Surveillance with serial echocardiography and vascular imaging plus interferon-signature monitoring for progression
Coordinated care through immunology or rheumatology, cardiology, dentistry and orthopaedics
Genetic counselling and family testing for the IFIH1 or DDX58 gain-of-function variant
